messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 69

# The Weight of What the Body Remembers

Priya is a 45-year-old South Asian woman who has worked as a plumber for nearly two decades. She is the kind of person who has always prided herself on being capable — someone who can diagnose a problem, get under a sink, and fix what is broken. She has built her small business with her hands, and for a long time, her body felt like something she could rely on absolutely.

Three years ago, that changed.

It began with fatigue she attributed to overwork, then a persistent pain in her abdomen she assumed was stress. By the time she went to the emergency room, her doctors discovered an aggressive form of ovarian cancer that had already progressed significantly. What followed were eight months of surgery, chemotherapy, and hospitalizations — a period Priya describes as feeling like she was "trapped inside a body that was trying to kill me." She remembers lying in the hospital during her third round of chemotherapy, genuinely uncertain whether she would survive the week. A nurse told her, gently, to prepare her family for the possibility that she might not make it home. Priya called her mother that night and said goodbye.

She did survive. Her cancer is currently in remission. But the woman who came home from the hospital is not quite the same woman who walked into the emergency room.

Priya returned to work about fourteen months ago, and on the surface, she has rebuilt much of her life. She takes on jobs, manages her schedule, and shows up. But inside, something remains fractured. Several nights a week she wakes between two and four in the morning, heart pounding, certain that something is catastrophically wrong. The dreams are vivid — she is back in the hospital bed, watching an IV drip, unable to move or speak while doctors talk around her as though she is already gone. She lies awake for hours afterward, running her hands over her abdomen, checking for pain.

During the day, her body keeps its own kind of vigil. Any physical sensation — a cramp, a headache, an unfamiliar ache from a long day of work — sends her into a spiral of dread that can last for hours. She has gone to her GP four times in the past six months for symptoms that turned out to be benign. She knows, intellectually, that this is happening. She cannot stop it. When she is crawling through a tight crawlspace or cutting pipe, her mind will suddenly return to the hospital without warning — the smell of the ward, the cold weight of the IV needle, the sound of the monitor beside her bed. She has to stop what she is doing and breathe until the present comes back.

Priya has become quieter socially. She was once close to a group of friends from her community, but she finds gatherings exhausting in a way she struggles to articulate. People ask how she is doing and she says fine, because the truth — that she is terrified every single day that the cancer will return, that she no longer trusts her own body, that she sometimes feels she is living on borrowed time that could be revoked without notice — feels too large and too frightening to put into a conversation over dinner.

She is single, and she lives alone, which means that most nights the fear has no company. She keeps the television on when she sleeps, not for entertainment but for noise — proof that the world is still moving, that she is still in it.

What Priya finds most difficult to explain is this: she survived. She knows she is supposed to feel grateful. And she does, in moments. But survival did not return her to who she was before. Some part of her remains in that hospital room, listening to her own heartbeat and waiting to find out whether it will stop.
